response:
ACCEPTI find no blocking mathematical gap in the new low-congestion route-cover note. The  $m$ -layer circulation argument, preservation of saturated resource sinks, average cost after recombination, sharp excess bound, and switching counterexample are correct. The exact reservation theorem also holds for every stated  $W,d,q$ : the supplied coordinates give an exhaustive symbolic description of the reachable terminal network.I inspected the supplied checker, report and Lean source as evidence. I did not execute them or independently confirm the reported runs. The mathematical acceptance below does not rely on extrapolating from those runs or on the prior parity review.The minimal edits I recommend are clarifications: explicitly discard the auxiliary return arc before cycle removal; qualify the unique-continuation statement by excluding mixed-owner self-links; and replace “interval endpoints” with “interval units” in the reservation sharpness argument.1. The  $m$ -layer lower-bounded-circulation proof is validThe aggregate arc bound is justifiedLet  $F$  be the sum of the  $mk$  supplied route occurrences. The following are distinct facts, and the proof establishes each:Every source boundary arc has flow  $m$ .Every mixed split arc has flow  $\ell(u)\le m$ .Every resource sink arc has flow  $\ell(u)\le m$ .Every individual witnessed link or access arc has flow at most  $m$ .The last point follows from conservation at its tail. An alpha node receives exactly  $m$  units through its source boundary arc. A mixed exit receives at most  $m$  through its split arc. Each outgoing arc carries at most that total throughput. Thus
$$0\le F_e\le m$$
on all original network arcs, including the witnessed arcs that had capacity  $k+1$  in the single-packing normal form.This does not confuse the aggregate certificate with a feasible single packing. The aggregate uses capacity  $m$ ; each layer will use capacity one.The induction works even when a residual contains cyclesFor clarity, write  $r$  for the current residual multiplicity and  $G$  for the current residual flow. The induction invariant is:
$$\operatorname{val}(G)=rk,\qquad
0\le G_e\le r,\qquad
G_{\text{source boundary}}=r,$$
with  $G$  integral and conserved at all internal vertices.For  $r>1$ , impose
$$\max\{0,G_e-(r-1)\}\le f_e\le \min\{1,G_e\}.$$
The fractional flow  $G/r$  satisfies these bounds. Because  $G_e$  is integral, the cases are exactly: $G_e=0$ : both bounds are zero; $1\le G_e\le r-1$ : the bounds are zero and one; $G_e=r$ : both bounds are one.Adding the return arc  $t\to s$ , fixed at  $k$ , turns this into a feasible circulation with integral lower and upper bounds. The invoked integrality theorem applies exactly in this setting: feasibility with integral bounds implies integral feasibility. A standard reference is Chekuri’s Combinatorial Optimization notes, §5.3.2, Theorems 5.16–5.17. courses.physics.illinois.eduDiscarding that auxiliary return arc gives an integral value- $k$  flow  $f$  in the original network. The remainder satisfies
$$0\le G_e-f_e\le r-1,$$
has value  $(r-1)k$ , and has flow  $r-1$  on each source boundary arc. Thus the induction continues. At  $r=1$ , take the remaining flow as the last layer.Nothing in this induction requires  $G$  to remain a sum of the original intact routes. Conservation, integrality and the arc bounds suffice. In particular, retaining circulation cycles throughout peeling is legitimate and preserves the exact identity
$$F=f^{(1)}+\cdots+f^{(m)}$$
before the final cycle removals.2. Cycle removal, resource preservation and cost are compatibleSaturated resource sinks survive in every layerIf a resource  $u$  has  $\ell(u)=m$ , its sink arc satisfies
$$\sum_{j=1}^{m}f^{(j)}_u=m,
\qquad
f^{(j)}_u\in\{0,1\}.$$
Therefore every layer uses that sink arc once.After the auxiliary return arc has been discarded, the original super-sink has no outgoing arc. Hence its incoming resource sink arcs cannot lie on directed cycles. Removing cycles therefore preserves their flow. The same reasoning applies to source boundary arcs, since the original super-source has no incoming arc.The distinction in the manuscript is consequently correct:Arc typeCan lie on an original directed cycle?Saturation necessarily survives cycle deletion?Source boundaryNoYesResource sinkNoYesInternal mixed splitYesNo such conclusion followsThe proof does not silently promote resource preservation into mixed-owner preservation. Deleting a cycle may lower the use of a saturated mixed split arc, which is allowed by the theorem’s final “combined use at most” conclusion.Each resulting layer is a legal complete packingCycle deletion preserves the value  $k$ . Decomposing the resulting integral flow into paths gives exactly  $k$  paths. All  $k$  source boundary arcs are occupied, so every source appears once.The mixed split capacities prevent two paths from using the same mixed owner. The sink capacities prevent two paths from using the same original resource, including two different BP presentations of one beta owner.Recombination is compatible with terminal witnesses. At a mixed owner, every incoming link uses its unique BP terminal and every outgoing link uses its unique TP terminal. Switching between a certificate prefix and another certificate suffix therefore retains valid witnessed terminal links. Source and beta capacities handle their two-terminal presentations, while the separately stated cap-witness nonconflict hypothesis handles the physical access adapter.Thus the construction gives the asserted legal packings, without needing an intact candidate-route selection.Averaging and preservation refer to the same packingsLet  $c_j$  be the cost of the  $j$ -th packing after cycle removal. Arc use only decreases, and all link costs are nonnegative, so
$$\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_j\le L.$$
Consequently,
$$\min_j c_j\le \left\lfloor\frac Lm\right\rfloor.$$
Every one of these packings preserves every saturated resource sink. Therefore the packing selected by the averaging argument preserves them too. There is no mismatch between the family of packings used to prove preservation and the family used to prove the cost bound.Minimal clarification: insert the sentence:Discard the auxiliary return arc before removing directed cycles in the original network.The current wording about the “original super-sink” already signals this interpretation, so I do not regard its omission as a blocking gap.3. The excess deficit bound and its sharpness are correctFor each separator  $Z$ , every supplied occurrence from every source in  $U_Z$  must meet  $Z$ . Otherwise that occurrence itself would survive as a route to a surviving resource.Counting occurrences, including repeated copies, therefore gives
$$m|U_Z|
\le \sum_{u\in Z}\ell(u)
\le m|Z|+\sum_{u\in Z}(\ell(u)-m)_+
\le m|Z|+E_m.$$
It follows that
$$m\bigl(|U_Z|-|Z|\bigr)\le E_m.$$
The supplied normal-form separator formula is appropriate here:
$$\delta=\max_Z\bigl(|U_Z|-|Z|\bigr).$$
Its minimum-cut argument is sound. A minimum cut has capacity at most  $k$ , so it cuts no witnessed arc of capacity  $k+1$ . Its remaining cut arcs identify excluded sources and actual mixed/resource capacity objects. The sources on the source side become blocked after those objects are removed, giving the required reverse inequality.Taking the maximum yields
$$m\delta\le E_m,
\qquad
\delta\le\left\lfloor\frac{E_m}{m}\right\rfloor.$$
There is no double charging of excess. An occurrence meeting several objects in  $Z$  contributes several terms to the right side of the incidence inequality, making that side larger. Each capacity object’s excess still enters  $E_m$  exactly once.The normal-form normalization needed to interpret  $\delta$  as unpaid compensation is also sound: compressed components alternate alpha and beta owners; an interval-paid component has an end alpha accessible through the chosen free-TP tail; reserving that tail leaves a balanced alternating path. The selected segments use a subset of the original cancellation links.SharpnessIn the shared-mixed-owner example,
$$\ell(\text{mixed gate})=mk,
\qquad
\ell(\text{each interval})=1.$$
Since  $m\ge1$ , the intervals contribute no excess, and
$$E_m=mk-m=m(k-1).$$
The shared gate permits exactly one routed source, so
$$\nu=1,\qquad \delta=k-1.$$
Equality holds for every claimed  $m\ge1$  and  $k\ge2$ .The abstract-only scope is correctly stated. The example does not need a rectangular-grid realization.For  $m=2$ , the consequence  $E_2\le1\Rightarrow\delta=0$  follows immediately from integrality. The note correctly refrains from extending its cost and saturated-resource conclusions to arbitrary positive-excess certificates.4. The switching counterexample is validThe four supplied candidates have

\qquad
\ell(R_A)=\ell(R_B)=2.$$
Every supplied  $A$ -route intersects every supplied  $B$ -route in a mixed owner: $uv$  intersects  $ux$  at  $u$ , and  $vy$  at  $v$ ; $xy$  intersects  $ux$  at  $x$ , and  $vy$  at  $y$ .Thus selecting one intact supplied candidate for each source is impossible.The switched routes
$$A\to x\to R_B,
\qquad
B\to v\to R_A$$
use witnessed arcs present in the certificate union. They have disjoint mixed owners, distinct resources and total link cost two. The four original candidates each have two link arcs, so their total cost is eight and the theorem’s average bound is four.For completeness, an explicit full two-layer decomposition is:LayerRoute from  $A$ Route from  $B$ Total cost1 $A\to u\to x\to R_B$  $B\to v\to y\to R_A$ 42 $A\to x\to y\to R_B$  $B\to u\to v\to R_A$ 4Together these layers use exactly the certificate’s witnessed arc multiplicities.There is a useful distinction here: the particular cost-two repair does not extend to a full two-layer decomposition dominated by this certificate. Once its source departures  $A\to x$  and  $B\to v$  are used, the two remaining source departures both enter  $u$ . That prevents a second complete packing.This is not a defect in the note. Theorem 1 guarantees the existence of suitable layers and a cheap layer among them; it does not guarantee that every cheap packing in the union can be extended to such a decomposition. The displayed cost-two packing is used only to demonstrate the benefit of switching.The checker’s finite terminal realization matches the prose: its six owners are  $A,B,u,v,x,y$ , and its link and access lists provide the stated candidates and repair.5. $$B_s^+,\ B_s^-$$
be the two three-unit branch sets for source  $s$ .Deleting routing capacities cannot introduce new routes. By the exhaustive description above,  $s$  can be paid exactly when at least one branch avoids  $F$ . Because branch capacities are disjoint across sources, one can choose a surviving branch independently for every payable source. Therefore
$$\delta(F)

and
$$\nu(F)=k-\delta(F).$$
Every surviving route has cost two. Hence
$$\min\{\text{route cost at value }\nu(F)\}=2\nu(F).$$
The normal-form cost equivalence transfers this to cancellation and allocation within the declared terminal model: an arbitrary admissible cancellation cannot attain the same payment with fewer links than its normalized routes.For every blocked source,  $F$  contains one unit from each of two disjoint branches. for every  $0\le s\le k$ .
